subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   FOOD AND DRUGS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Bill before us today clearly and simply proposes the full labelling of all restaurant meals. This sounds relatively uncomplicated as proposed in this Bill, but as so often happens, plans that look simple on paper are not always practical in the real world. Let us consider for a few moments the effect such a labelling requirement could have on the restaurant industry.
Most restaurant owners are proud of their establishment and try to serve the best food possible at the most reasonable price possible, while still ensuring some profit. Accordingly, they deal with a number of suppliers and buy from the source with the best product at the best price. This would, of course, be no problem if all products of a similar nature were identical. However, we are talking about the real world. For example, let us examine the potential problems with something as simple as flour.
Under Canadian food and drug regulations there are nine food additives permitted in flour for use as bleaching, naturing and dough conditioning agents. Of course, not all of those food additives would be used in a particular flour at the same time, but they provide the manufacturer with optional ingredients any one of which can be selected based on availability, price and technical requirements. The use of flour from one source with a certain combination of ingredients and food additives is no problem for the restauranteur.
When his supply runs low, however, he must either order more flour with the same composition from the same supplier, which limits his ability to shop around and get the best price available, or order flour with perhaps slightly different components from somewhere else. In the latter case, he is faced with having to change the ingredient and food additive information on every dish in which flour is used in his restaurant. The cost of changing this information would no doubt result in higher prices in the restaurant. If he decides not to change suppliers, he becomes tied to one supplier and as a
result may very well wind up paying a higher price for the same flour. That again would require raising the prices in his establishment.
This is only one ingredient out of hundreds that a restaurant would use in the course of its business. The very same factors would apply to a majority, if not all, of foods and would create the need for tremendous record keeping efforts by both the restauranteur and the wholesaler.
In another situation, it is conceivable that the chef could run out of one ingredient such as a spice mixture while preparing a meal. Under this Bill he would not be able to substitute another mixture without changing the ingredient listing and, subsequently the preparation of the meal could be delayed or the food wasted and the service time for the consumer prolonged considerably.
There could also be considerably less creativity by chefs if complete ingredient labelling were required. Can you imagine the indignation of a master chef who has just finished creating a new gourmet meal when he is told that his masterpiece cannot be served to the public until the new ingredient listings are printed and ready for distribution? In fact, there may be great reluctance on the part of great chefs to reveal all the ingredients in their sauces and other foods.
Let us reflect for a moment on the dimension of the problem addressed here today. This is important if a practical solution is to be found. It needs to be recognized that not all ingredients are associated with severe adverse reactions. In fact, of the multitude of foods and food ingredients, only a small number have been associated with frequent or severe adverse reactions in susceptible individuals.
If this Bill before us today is passed it will create severe problems in the food industry as well as tremendous difficulties for the individual restauranteur. It is quite possible that it would produce so much labelling information that the sensitive consumer may not be able to comprehend all of it. That is not to say, however, that some measures are not required to provide to the consumer more information on the presence of potential allergens in foods.
To this end, officials of the Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare, in conjunction with representatives from the Canadian Restaurant and Food Services Association and the Allergy Information Association, have developed a proposal to address this situation. A list of the allergens responsible for the most severe or most frequent adverse reactions has been prepared and is presently being reviewed by the medical profession. As a first step, it is planned that a chart be made available to the consumer with information on the presence of these selected allergens in the foods served in fast service food establishments.
This proposal is far more practical and beneficial to all parties than the Bill before us today. Furthermore, the Allergy Information Association, having broad experience and contact with Canadians who suffer from adverse reactions to foods,
September 26, 1988

drugs, et cetera, as well as the Canadian Diabetics Association, many of whose members manage institutional and commercial food services, have indicated support for this step-wise approach. Therefore, if this Bill were to pass it would seriously damage the productive negotiations between the Health Protection Branch and the food service industry to address this problem.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   FOOD AND DRUGS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the first comprehensive regulations governing the labelling of food products were introduced in the early 60's under the Food and Drugs Act.
The Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is responsible for enforcing the provisions relating to labelling, packaging and advertising of food products, under the Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act, the Food and Drugs Act and the regulations made therunder.
The Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare advises the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affaires on labelling and advertising matters relating to health. In 1973, the Departement of Consumer and Corporate Affairs published draft regulations on the packaging and labelling of consumer products as well as proposed amendments to the Food and Drugs regulations substantially changing food labelling requirements.
Madam Speaker, the new regulations were promulgated in 1974 and manufacturers of foods products were given a period of two years in order to implement them. These regulations gave rise to a comprehensive set of rules and guidelines relating to labelling and advertising.
Prepackaged foods must now bear a label with the following information, which is important: common name of the food, net contents, name and address of the person responsible for the product, a list of ingredients, durable life date and, if required, instructions for proper storage.
All the information required must be in English and French, except the name and address of the manufacturer which can be in either language.
Regarding more particularly the list of ingredients, these must be mentioned on most prepackaged foods in decreasing order of quantity or percentage of the prepackaged product. However, there are some exceptions, namely the following:
First, products that are prepackaged on retail premises; second, prepackaged individual portions of food that are served by a restaurant or other commercial enterprise with meals or snacks; third, prepackaged individual servings of food that are prepared by a commissary and sold by automatic vending machines or mobile canteens; four, meat and meat by-products that are barbecued, roasted or broiled on the retail premises; also, standardised alcoholic beverages and vinegars.
Some ingredients may be shown at the end of the list in any order. Those ingredients, Madam Speaker, can be spices,
Food and Drugs Act
seasonings, herbs, except table salt, natural or artificial flavours, flavour enhancers, additives, vitamins, salts or derivatives of vitamins, mineral nutrients and salts of mineral nutrients.
Ingredients must generally be shown by their common names. Some of them, however, such as vegetable oils, flavours, seasonings, milk products may be identified by the name of the food category they represent.
Meat, poultry, fish or their by-products must be identified by their individual names, and in the case of vegetable protein based products, the source of the protein must be specifically identified on the label.
In the case of optional ingredients, or those that can be substituted to others in the preparation of a product, the label may list all ingredients that could be included in the product during the year. However, it must be clearly indicated those ingredients may not necessarily be present in a given package of that food.
Besides, when an ingredient has several components, the complete list of those components must appear on the label unless otherwise excepted by Food and Drug Regulations. Among ingredients for which a list of components is not mandatory we could mention butter, flour and cheese. Apart from the information processors must provide on the label, they can choose to list a certain number of additional information about their products. To protect consumers against any possibility of misleading information, guidelines were developed for the categories of statements that may legitimately appear on labels.
As pointed out, Madam Speaker, none of those labelling provisions apply to food served in restaurants, hotels or other food service outlets. And a close look at conditions in restaurants shows how impractical it would be to put them under such vast regulations. Some restaurants for instance serve a whole range of foods and sometimes change from day to day their menus and even their individual recipes. What would happen to small roadside snackbars and take-out restaurants with limited resources? How could they obey such labelling provisions? Further, trying to impose regulations without at the same time educating the food service industry, including for instance suppliers, and an adequate enforcing mechanism? This might expose sensitive consumers to a higher risk situation than now prevails. Also, if we were to force restaurateurs to label their foods, this would have to be done in a way that would not entertain a feeling of false security among people with food allergies. For the time being, it is therefore imperative that people with those kinds of allergies do not hesitate to inquire with the restaurateur about the ingredients of the foods before eating them.
Where the specific substance responsible for the allergic reaction is present in the food, or where the restaurateur does not seem to be quite sure of the exact ingredients, the consumer should not hesitate for a moment to stay away from both that food and that restaurant. People with food allergies

September 26, 1988
Food and Drugs Act
should understand it is their responsibility to do everything in their power to avoid the substance to which they are allergic. This however does not relieve food service operations from the responsibility to better inform their customers to the best of their knowledge as to the ingredients of the foods they serve, when asked to do so.
Indeed, officials from the Health Protection Branch in the Department of National Health and Welfare are actively discussing with representatives of the restaurant and food services industry, the Allergy Information Association and the medical profession to exactly determine what information should be easily accessible to consumers as well as the best ways to make it available. Let me suggest, Madam Speaker, that we should simply let those people go about their work, without government interference.

I will be very brief in my comments, Mr. Speaker. I hope this Bill will be passed this afternoon and then go on to committee where it can be studied in greater detail. Witnesses can appear and discuss the important aspects of the legislation.
I strongly support the thrust of this legislation. Indeed, I want to take this opportunity to congratulate the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) who brought the Bill before the House and I believe as well the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) who has also spoken out on this issue in the past, as has my colleague the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) and a number of colleagues from the New Democratic Party.
I myself have received letters from a number of constituents on the subject matter of this Bill. A Mrs. Gail Takeshita of Sussex Avenue in Burnaby wrote a letter as follows:
Dear Mr. Robinson:
As a parent of a child with very severe food allergies, I was pleased to receive a letter.. . informing me of.. . Bill C-289 in an effort to achieve legislation requiring disclosure of ingredients in restaurant foods.
My daughter has "anaphylaxis" which can also be called "allergic shock" or "general allergic reaction". This is a life-threatening reaction to foods. Incorrect information given by a waiter or waitress, or improper or inadequate ingredient listing on a package could someday cost my daughter her life.
Mrs. Takeshita strongly supports this legislation, and understandably so because the life of her child is at risk.
As well, I received a letter from a Rev. Sam Smith, an elderly gentleman who lives in South Burnaby. He writes to me about a situation facing his family particularly with respect to monosodium glutamate. He points out:
Monosodium glutamate is the most dangerous. Causing allergic reactions in
about 50 per cent of Canadians, to a more or less degree.
I believe my colleague from Vancouver East has indicated she is one of the Canadians who responds in a negative way to
MSG. Rev. Smith points out that his wife can go into convulsions if she gets the amount of MSG considered normal in prepared foods. The worst foods are those in which the makers consider MSG to be only a flavour enhancer and therefore do not even list it as an ingredient.
The purpose of this legislation is straightforward. The Member for Hamilton East noted that she was certainly prepared to accept that there were some difficulties in the drafting of the Bill, but that in principle the legislation should go forward to committee. The key point is that now if one goes into a grocery store to purchase food, one is entitled by law to a listing of the ingredients in that food. However, if one goes into a fast food restaurant, a McDonalds, an Arby's, a Wendy's, there is no similar requirement. I would hope this House at this very late stage in this Parliament, perhaps the last week in which this Parliament is sitting, could in fact move in an non-partisan spirit together to pass this important piece of legislation.
I would hope as well that it would be recognized that it has the support of the Consumers' Association of Canada, the Ontario Medical Association and a number of other medical associations and, I believe, the Canadian Council on Children and Youth has examined this question. I would hope this Bill could be moved forward, the committee could examine it with care this week and it could be adopted before the House rises at the end of this week.
I support the legislation. I believe it is legislation that will be of benefit to literally millions of Canadians. I would hope the House would adopt the Bill in principle this afternoon.

I feel he is right but we have been wrong so many other Fridays over the past months, I do not quite have his confidence. However, I think the Bill should be put to a vote shortly. I have been impressed by certain statistics that are available to us from the Good Housekeeping Institute. The report is from a survey taken by that body with respect to concern over reaction to chemicals used in food, snacks and soft drinks. It was ranked second by consumers as being a matter of great concern and danger. Clearly, there is not only a concern on the part of people across North America, but it is a concern that is substantiated by the serious threat to health, indeed, to life,

from the failure to have available the kind of information which this Bill wishes to put before the public.
We have to appreciate that if one suffers from this or that allergy, eating the wrong food can inflict not only discomfort but actual illness or possibly even death, so that a person who knows he or she has these allergies lives under the constant threat of taking the wrong food at a reception, a party, in a restaurant or wherever. There is no way that any individual given those circumstances is going to be wholly safe. We should take whatever steps we can take to bring to those people as much safety as we can. That is really the intention, as I understand it, of the legislation before us.
I commend the Hon. Member for Hamilton East who has brought it to the House. It shows the great value of Private Member's Bills. We private Members can focus the attention of Parliament on something that otherwise would be ignored. We can use this greatest forum of the land to be sure that the nation as a whole is aware that a problem is being taken seriously, that a solution is being examined responsibly.
Debate has already illustrated some of the difficulties of implementing such a Bill as we are considering. One difficulty is the fact that there are widely varying estimates about the number of people who suffer allergies. Some say there are three million in the United States alone. Some say there are 20 million in the United States alone. Whatever the number may be, we know there is a vast array of people who live under constant threat that at least their health is threatened and possibly their life by eating the wrong food.
We do not have precise statistics, but do we need them? Are we not aware that this is a commonly felt problem? Are there any of us who do not know someone who suffers from this or that allergy? They may be allergic to an element in food or to something in the atmosphere. I think all of us are aware of people, sometimes very close to us, who suffer from allergies and need this kind of protection. I can think of one time in the life of my oldest child when she was very, very young. It seemed that almost in a matter of minutes her life was threatened because she was allergic to an element she had taken into her body. If we had not been able to rush her to a hospital and have her receive treatment, she would not have lived another hour. The memory of that traumatic afternoon when the seemingly unbelievable was real before our eyes has certainly made me sensitive to the subject before us.
A little girl was playing as any other little girl might be, and then suddenly she was not able to breathe and had to be rushed to a hospital, we wondered for what reason, and then we were told what the reason was. Fortunately, treatment was a hand. But it has certainly made me sensitive to the critical nature of what we are debating.
When we focus attention, as we are right to do, on the difficulties in implementing this legislation, I hope we will give at least equal attention to the difficulty of living without it. Let us ask about the security of people if they do not have this kind of protection. We are now living in a time when it is needed
Food and Drugs Act
more than ever. We now live in a time when so many people eat so many meals out. As a boy, I remember that going out for a meal out was an event. It is now commonplace. There are fast food restaurants, gourmet restaurants, and all the eating places in between. The fact is that many people are taking a large number of their meals out, some are taking most of their meals out and some, perhaps, all of them. More than ever throughout the western world we are subject to the possibility of being allergic to food in a meal the elements of which are unknown to us. If a person is unfortunate enough to have those allergies that can threaten health or even life, then this is a matter of great crisis.
In general, I support the intention of this legislation. I would like briefly to conclude by citing three steps I think we must take to cope with the problem. The first step is education. We are doing some of that right now. I look upon the House of Commons as a place of education as well as of legislation. It is a forum in which the representatives of the people of Canada debate with one another and put before the people of Canada the great issues of their time. This is such an issue when it affects the lives of people. We need more education to arouse awareness, to strengthen consciousness, so that everyone connected with providing a food to the public will see the serious nature of what we are talking about.
Second, this Bill is about communication, about the most effective way of communicating to people the knowledge necessary for health and life.
Finally, I want to take a moment to dwell on the need for regulation. We need law because we are humans. We do not always respond to good advice, to good counsel, to good information. We should but we do not. So many of us need the law to prod, to force, and so we move from education, which is always the best, the first and, I hope, long step.
We move to the step of regulation. The intent of this Bill, as I understand it, is to provide that measure of regulation which will provide a measure of security, which is surely the right of every Canadian if it can be provided.
I look upon this Bill as an effort at legitimate regulation. I do not quarrel with having traffic police that tell us to drive this way and sometimes to drive that way, to slow down, to speed up. We need that kind of regulating on the roads. We need regulating when it comes to putting up buildings.
I have just had an experience within the past month or so of dealing with municipal authorities over building regulations. They are quite right. For the protection of all, for the public good, we need processes through which we are required to go. Here we have another example of the same thing, a need for regulation in the public domain, regulation in the places to which men, women, and children are required to go day by day, namely, where they can find food and sustenance for life itself.

Food and Drugs Act
It has been said that man is what he eats. If that is the case, legislation dealing with the regulating of food is certainly among the basic legislation that can be put before this Parliament. I believe that we have a serious intent of that. This Bill certainly deserves to go to committee and I hope that detailed study will return to this House a Bill that is workable and that will improve the lot of our fellow Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I would like to comment very briefly on Bill C-289 which I supported during the debate on June 9 this year, when the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) introduced this Bill.
The purpose of the Bill is to compel restaurants to make available for public consultation a list, in English or in French, of all the ingredients in any food sold by them. I will continue to read from the Explanatory Notes to the Bill:
This Bill will also compel each branch restaurant to affix on the packaging
of any packaged food sold by it a list, in English and in French, of the
ingredients in such food.
Madam Speaker, this proposal was introduced by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East, and I think it is an excellent idea. Personally, I know people who are allergic to nuts and sea food or who, like me, are allergic to the hair of animals like cats, dogs, and all that sort of thing. I get asthma, so I know how I react and what I should avoid.
In this case, we are talking mostly about young people who eat outside the home and occasionally eat a hasty meal in a fast food establishment such as McDonald's, Harvey's and so forth. These young people must have access to a list of the ingredients they ingest. This may be extremely important, because as anyone who is allergic to something will understand, it is not always obvious that the cake or bread or food a person is served contains a specific ingredient, added during the cooking or preparation of the food, that acts as an irritant to that person and may cause a very strong allergic reaction.
I remember a very awkward situation when one of my friends who was allergic to nuts ordered a piece of cake. He specifically asked the waitress whether there were any nuts in the cake, and the waitress said no, there were none. He ate a piece and in fact, there was a dusting of ground nuts on the cake, and I have seldom seen such a violent reaction. He sort of choked and said, "There are nuts in it. Something's wrong." So something had to be done right away. He had to be taken to the hospital and given emergency treatment.
I am very impressed by these people who suffer from allergies and who sometimes have to deal with very difficult situations because of this lack of information. It seems quite right and straightforward to me that the House pass this Bill on second reading and send it to a committee in order to be able to really deal with the challenge raised by requiring fast food outlets and restaurants that are becoming increasingly popular with young people to describe on the box or container what is inside. I think that McDonald's, for example, has
agreed to do so voluntarily. I am told that other chains will do so as a matter of good public relations and probably out of concern for the public welfare, but I think that this subject is important enough to justify sending the Bill for a thorough analysis of the consequences and to really see whether the Minister is right in saying that it would be onerous, difficult and sometimes impossible for food chains to list the ingredients on the container of the products they sell. I am not too satisfied with the Minister's answer that it is too onerous when we see one of the major chains, McDonald's, offer to do what the Bill proposes, i.e. describe on the container or warn the consumer what he or she is about to consume.
Madam Speaker, this Bill can be justified for all sorts of reasons, and not the least is the Canadian statistics showing that one Canadian a month dies of an allergic reaction to certain foods. So, it is a mattter of concern for me and I think that it is important for us to give it serious consideration and to refer this Bill immediately to the committee who may see fit to hear experts and representatives from the food chains concerned explain to us why and how we could implement a system which would enable us to meet the requirements of the law and which would inform Canadians by giving them a list of the ingredients of the products they are about to eat, whether out of a box or in restaurants. I for one will give support to that Bill and I hope that my colleagues in this House will do the same.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I take this opportunity to offer a few comments on Private Member's Bill C-289 which, as you know, is an Act to amend the Food and Drugs Act concerning the listing of ingredients contained in restaurant food. It would compel every restaurant to make available to the public a list, in English or in French, of all the ingredients in any food it sells.
This is certainly a very sensitive issue. It has received a great deal of attention from health professionals, food regulators, the media, and the public at large. This attention is very well justified. Tragic deaths have resulted from allergic reactions to restaurant food, particularly in the so-called fast food restaurants.
According to various news reports, some 25,000 Canadians are at risk every day because of their food allegies. Some 24 people in Canada have died over the past two years, one a month, because of allergic reactions to food eaten in restaurants.
I am one of those unfortunate Canadians who suffers from a food allergy. I am sure that my colleagues on all sides of the House will be happy to know that my allergy is not life threatening. However, that is not quite so with one of my daughters who, over time, has developed an allergy to just one element that we have been able to determine, peanut and peanut oil, which can appear without warning as an ingredient. In her case, her sensitivity has developed to a degree where it
September 26, 1988

requires only the most minute amount for her to have a very serious allergic reaction. Of course this is of great concern to me and the rest of our family and to any other Canadian who might have that kind of allergy.
Therefore, I welcome this initiative to try to deal with this matter so that Canadians do not unnecessarily expose themselves to risk.
It is not possible to indemnify a Canadian at all times from such risks if he or she has had the misfortune of developing a reaction. But certainly we as parliamentarians can go as far as reasonably possible to assist them in staying healthy.
It is very heartening to note that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) is well aware of the problem of the allergic reaction to restaurant food and has already issued instructions to his Department to determine how much, if any, of an increase in food sensitivity reactions there has been, whether a perceived increase might be due to the availability of better instrumentation and diagnosis, and whether the population as a whole is becoming more sensitive for one reason or another. These are important scientific facts that must be determined in examining a reasonable solution.
In addition, the House of Commons Standing Committee on National Health and Welfare has held hearings on the feasibility of mandatory labelling for food products sold in restaurants and fast food outlets. Our Government is determined to find the best possible solution to the problem. It is likely that a large proportion of food sensitivity reactions are linked to relatively few foods or food components. On the other hand, almost any food has the potential to trigger a serious allergic reaction in an occasionally sensitive individual.
This problem is quite complex, and it is vital to solicit input from all parties concerned. Officials from Health and Welfare Canada and the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs have consulted with both the Canadian Food and Restaurant Association and the Allergy Information Association. Consensus has been reached that a chart identifying foods served in an establishment and an indication as to whether or not they contain substances for listing on a so-called priority list was perhaps the most suitable mechanism for providing the information required.
In this context it is appropriate to quote from a letter from Mr. Douglas Needham, Executive Vice-President of the Canadian Restaurant and Food Services Association. Mr. Needham writes that his association supports the consumer's right to know the ingredients used in restaurant meals, and that his association continues to work with all concerned groups to identify and implement measures that will decrease the likelihood of more tragic deaths.
I want to applaud Mr. Needham and his association on this stand. In fact, according to a recent report by the Canadian Press, the Canadian Restaurant and Food Services Association
Food and Drugs Act
is strongly encouraging a voluntary program among its 6,800 members. Industry spokespeople such as Mr. Needham have said that restaurant menus should warn consumers of ingredients that could lead to allergic reactions before they order a meal. The association has suggested a system of warning charts that could be introduced in quick service restaurant chains, because these establishments have a highly centralized control over ingredients.
The consistency of the menus in chain restaurants, combined with the limited choices available, make the charts a manageable idea. According to the same report by the Canadian Press, the association has talked with 24 quick service restaurant chains, and 22 of them have agreed to take part.
This is good news. It shows that the food industry is well aware of the problem and is more than willing to take steps to resolve it. It further shows that the idea of an ingredients list, if it can be fine-tuned and made manageable and practical is indeed a good one.
It is quite possible that the best way to protect Canadians with food allergies as they dine out is through the use of these ingredient lists. If this is the case, then every effort must be made to adopt the very best listing system possible. In this light, it seems quite probable that Bill C-289, effective as it has been in focusing attention on the problem, can be improved.
It is essential that consumers get the information they need to protect themselves in the marketplace, and to make intelligent choices. This applies as much to allergy sufferers who dine in restaurants as to anyone else.
The Government is determined to bring about an effective solution to this issue. If that solution is found to centre upon ingredient disclosure lists, then the House can be assured that the listing requirements will be applied in a manner that is effective, fair and as cost-efficient as possible.
Fast food and quick service restaurants are popular among Canadians, as we all know, and in large measure because quality control is strict. Consumers know what they are getting with a great deal of certainty, and prices are reasonable and affordable. We want to make sure that this continues.
We must adopt a system that affords the best possible protection to the Canadian consumer, and at the same time allows greater freedom and safety for those who suffer from food allergies. This is a very worth-while Bill. I certainly hope it gets to committee and is passed into law.

Madam Speaker, I regard Bill C-289 as a positive step to solve a very serious problem. I am happy to see that we, in Canada, already have legislation in that area. It gives us hope for a definite solution in the foreseeable future to the problem of allergic Canadians who, when they eat in a restaurant, run a risk of having violent or fatal reactions.

September 26, 1988
Food and Drugs Act
Under the Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act and Regulations and the Food and Drugs Act and Regulations, food companies must provide, in both official languages, comprehensive information on the foods they sell and on the ingredients in those foods. This is required for imported as well as Canadian products.
The Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act was passed in 1972 and it has had a tremendous effect. In general, suppliers know their obligations very well and put on their labels in both official languages the clear and precise information required by law. And we can say that, with some rare exceptions, offences are quickly dealt with.
That is fine for food products that Canadians buy in stores and put in their refrigerators. On the label of the canned ham or cereal box that he or she just bought, the consumer will find the product's generic name, the net quantity, the name and address of the company, the list of ingredients, the product's durability, as well as the method of preservation.
That is fine, Madam Speaker, and I am sure that such requirements have strongly contributed towards maintaining and improving the health of Canadians. But up until now the law has not protected people who go to restaurants and nothing imposes on restaurant owners to say what ingredients have gone into their foods. This is the basic purpose of the Bill now before you.
But to ensure that solutions are satisfactory and efficient, we must take into account the diversity and the breaking up of the Canadian restaurant industry. Let us not lose track of the fact that 78 per cent of the sales volume in the restaurant business goes to small private firms, often family businesses with a long tradition or, in some cases, ill-conceived and short-lived ventures. This last aspect complicates things even further for the legislator.
Restaurant services in Canada rely on some 72 000 commercial locations all across the country. Food products are served in a variety of settings and places: traditional restaurants, fast food outlets, banquet halls in hotels, catering services, cafeterias, schools, clubs, hospitals, planes, trains, boats and push-carts.
Restaurants use and interchange a staggering number of ingredients of all kinds and from all countries. Even restaurants with limited menus and fast-food restaurants can use up to a thousand ingredients. In the vast majority of cases, restaurants are at the mercy of their suppliers who can change certain ingredients without telling them. This further complicates the whole matter.
Meals served in restaurants cannot be compared to foodstuff bought at the grocery store. In large grocery stores, the consumer can pick up a package, read the label and put it back on the shelf if he is not satisfied with the product. In a restaurant, the customer does not know what ingredients are used in the dishes he orders.
Foods prepared in restaurants are quite different from those which are packaged for retail sale. Therefore, information on the ingredients used in them must be provided in a different way, although as adequately and efficiently as in the case of store-bought foods.
The information provided by restaurants must conform to certain basic criteria including timeliness: the restaurant must provide information on the ingredients used in making the dishes presently listed on its menu; accuracy: emphasis must be placed on ingredients which are known to provoke allergic reactions; precision: precise information must be provided to avoid any risk to the customer.
A few major restaurant chains have put out allergen tables and others will soon follow. This would seem to be a fair response to the rights of clients generally, and especially those who suffer from food allergies. This is an important step which deserves encouragement, and such initiatives are highly commendable.
However, Madam Speaker, we all know that conditions are altogether different in ordinary restaurants. Where the daily menu includes soup, dessert as well as vegetables and fruit in season, the chef changes menus and ingredients every day. We would be asking too much if that kind of establishment were expected to post a list prepared in advance, and we certainly do not want smaller restaurants to go under in the more or less distant future. That simply is not the objective of the Bill.
Madam Speaker, I also know that everything must be done to help a restaurant owner maintain and preserve the essential element of creativity on which rest the success and good name of his establishment. The same goes for restaurants featuring exotic dishes, and there is no need for me to stress the importance of Asian, Italian, Greek and other such restaurants. In the case of some other restaurants a menu might not be adequate and perhaps they would have to produce a 12- or 18-inch-thick recipe book. These establishments would be faced with an extremely complicated chore if they had to produce printed lists of ingredients.
In any case, allergy-prone clients looking over a list of ingredients might be lulled into a false sense of security. A simple distraction might cause an error and an extra ingredient can be added to a dish and lead to a feeling of sickness. No substitution nor any minor change would be allowed-utopian expectations if we consider the very nature of most restaurants.
Nor should we look only at restaurants in our quest for solutions to food allergy problems, Madam Speaker, for medical science might provide some of the answers even though experts are sometimes rather bewildered by the complexity of allergies in this sector where knowledge evolves so rapidly. There is such a wide variety of allergies that singling them out and identifying them to find antidotes is a gargantuan undertaking. If on top of that you consider that no two individuals will have the same allergic reaction to a given ingredient and that medical treatment cannot be identical, you are faced with an undescribable puzzle.
September 26, 1988

This is a multi-facetted problem, and we will eventually find adequate solutions only if all interested Parties keep on seeking them. The medical profession is already involved and we know that a number of other organizations, including the Canadian Restaurant and Foodservices Association, have officially indicated their interest in this vital matter. Finally, we know that Flealth and Welfare Canada as well as Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada officials continue to investigate all possible means of properly informing Canadians and helping people with allergies go to restaurants without fearing for their health.
I am convinced that Bill C-289 is another step towards better solutions to this kind of consumer problem.
